name: Inpainting and Canvas Expansion
title: Inpainting and Canvas Expansion
answer: Inpainting is the practice of regenerating a selected region of an existing image while leaving the rest untouched, and canvas expansion, sometimes called outpainting, extends an image beyond its original borders. Both sit inside generative illustration workflows, where an artist treats the image as a surface that can be edited in parts rather than only produced whole. The work covers retouching, removing unwanted objects, repairing damaged scans, changing a subject's clothing or expression, and turning a cropped composition into a wider one. It applies to photographs, paintings, concept art and product mockups alike.

Both sit inside generative illustration workflows, where an artist treats the image as a surface that can be edited in parts rather than only produced whole. The work covers retouching, removing unwanted objects, repairing damaged scans, changing a subject's clothing or expression, and turning a cropped composition into a wider one. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The task runs on diffusion models trained to fill masked areas, with the mask telling the model which pixels to replace and the surrounding pixels acting as context. Common interfaces include Adobe Photoshop's Generative Fill, Stable Diffusion's inpainting mode, and hosted services built on similar checkpoints. Canvas expansion usually needs a model that can accept a larger output size than its training resolution, so the software tiles or scales the work. Hardware ranges from a laptop with a consumer GPU to rented cloud compute, and the site currently tracks 1,000 live image generation models, many of which offer an inpainting or expansion mode.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts with a mask, drawn by hand or generated from a selection, a depth map or a segmentation model. The artist writes a prompt for the masked area alone, sets a strength or denoise value that controls how far the result may drift from the original pixels, and generates several candidates. Expansion adds a step: the canvas is enlarged, the new border is masked, and the prompt describes what should continue into it, often with a reference to the existing edge. The artist then composites, blends seams, and repeats at higher resolution until the join is not visible.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions turn on what the model was trained on and what the artist supplies as input. Inpainting a client's photograph can raise questions about the photographer's copyright and the subject's likeness rights, and expanding a known artwork into new territory can raise moral rights issues even where copyright has expired. Provenance tools such as C2PA content credentials and watermarking schemes are increasingly attached to generated output, though adoption is uneven. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, and any studio using these tools should expect the legal picture to keep moving.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward models that hold consistency across a whole canvas, so an expanded image keeps the same lighting, perspective and style as the original. Reference based methods, where the artist supplies a second image to guide the fill, are becoming standard, and interactive tools are moving closer to real time. Expect tighter integration with 3D and video pipelines, where the same fill logic extends a frame or a texture. The practical effect for illustrators is that the boundary between editing and generating keeps thinning.
